name: Finding Collaborators
title: Finding Collaborators
answer: Finding collaborators for a grant proposal means identifying the people whose skills, data, or facilities fill the gaps in your own team, and whose involvement strengthens the case you will make to a funder. It covers co-investigators, named personnel, subcontractors, and external advisors, and it starts well before the call deadline rather than after. The scope is narrower than general networking, because every name you add has to be justified in the proposal narrative and on the budget. It also runs the other way, since being found by a lead investigator is how many researchers first join a funded project.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Finding collaborators for a grant proposal means identifying the people whose skills, data, or facilities fill the gaps in your own team, and whose involvement strengthens the case you will make to a funder. It covers co-investigators, named personnel, subcontractors, and external advisors, and it starts well before the call deadline rather than after. The scope is narrower than general networking, because every name you add has to be justified in the proposal narrative and on the budget. It also runs the other way, since being found by a lead investigator is how many researchers first join a funded project.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The working infrastructure is mostly public record: funder award databases, institutional research profiles, preprint servers, and the literature itself.Persistent identifiers such as ORCID and institutional repositories keep those names attached to the right person across job moves. Email, video calls, and shared document drafts carry the conversation once a name becomes a candidate.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The practical method is to work backwards from the proposal's aims, listing the expertise each aim requires and then matching names to those requirements. Reading recent papers on the topic, including the claims extracted from them, shows who is active and what they have already established. A short first contact that states the call, the deadline, the role you have in mind, and what you would need from the collaborator saves everyone time. Fit is checked through prior joint work, complementary rather than overlapping skills, and whether the person has the capacity to deliver within the project period.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Collaboration brings obligations that outlast the proposal: authorship conventions, data sharing agreements, intellectual property terms, and institutional sign-off on the budget and the scope of work. Each named partner's employer usually has to approve the submission, and some funders limit how many proposals a person may appear on. Provenance matters when you cite a prospective collaborator's results, so link to the original paper rather than a summary of it. Personal data about candidates should be handled under the relevant institutional policy, and eligibility rules should be read at the source.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Funders are increasingly asking for evidence that a team was assembled deliberately, with named roles and a stated division of labour, rather than a list of familiar names. Consortia spanning countries and sectors are becoming more common, which raises the coordination burden and the value of people who have run such projects before. Machine-readable profiles and award histories make it easier to find partners outside your usual circle, including early career researchers and groups in under-represented regions. The likely direction is earlier and more structured team formation, with the collaborator search treated as part of the proposal work rather than a preliminary to it.
